19          Plaintiff J.O., by and through Danaa Carrillo, her mother (“Plaintiff”), brings this class

20 action against Bytedance Inc., Bytedance Ltd., TikTok Ltd., TikTok Inc., TikTok Pte. Ltd., and

21 TikTok U.S. Data Security, Inc. (collectively, “Defendants”) in her individual capacity and on

22 behalf of all others similarly situated (“Class Members”), and alleges, upon personal knowledge as

23 to her own actions, her counsels’ investigation, and upon information and belief as to all other

24 matters as follows.

25                                    NATURE OF THE ACTION

26          1.     Plaintiff brings this case to address Defendants’ unlawful practice of permitting and

27 encouraging Plaintiff and children under the age of 13 to create user accounts on the TikTok app for

28 the purpose of collecting Personally Identifiable Information (“PII”). Defendants have knowingly

                                        CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT

 1 collected this PII and other intrusive data points without the children’s parents’ knowledge or
 2 consent. Defendants utilize this unlawfully collected PII to provide personally curated content to
 3 keep children engaged with TikTok for their own profit. Defendants share Plaintiff and other
 4 children’s PII with third parties and further curate their For You Pages with copious amounts of
 5 curated advertisements. Defendants have been on notice that their actions are unlawful since March
 6 27, 2019 1, when the United States Government issued a permanent injunction and a Civil Penalty
 7 against them, which prohibits Defendants from their collection and use of the personal information
 8 of children without verifiable parental consent.
 9           2.     Defendants own and control htps://www.tiktok.com and the associated TikTok App,

10 (“TikTok”) which utilizes a For You Page that operates by collecting PII and other sensitive data
11 points about users to appeal to each specific user and include videos and advertisements curated
12 towards that individual. Defendants’ business model and social media platform is particularly
13 attractive to minor children, and they routinely encourage and allow children under the age of 13 to
14 create and use TikTok accounts without their parents’ knowledge or consent and continuously fail
15 to comply with parents’ requests to delete their children’s accounts and personal information.
16           3.     Unbeknownst to Plaintiff, the minor children, and their parents, Defendants were

17 collecting and tracking PII and other sensitive information without providing direct notice or
18 gaining their parents’ verifiable consent in violation of the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act
19 of 1998 (“COPPA”) and Children’s Online Privacy Protection Rule, a federal statute and regulation
20 that protect children’s privacy and safety online.
21           4.     Plaintiff and minor children used the TikTok app and website in its intended form as

22 a social media platform, collecting data and PII to curate a For You Page despite being underaged

24 online from their children; (iv)failing to inform parents how Defendants utilize the information they
25 collect; and (v) failing to obtain verifiable consent from parents to collect, use, or disclose their
26 children’s PII.

 5                                COMMON FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS

 6       A. Defendants are aware their actions are in violation of COPPA

 7          33.     In February 2019, the United States Department of Justice filed a complaint against

 8 TikTok’s predecessors, Musical.ly and Musical.ly, Inc., alleging violations of the COPPA Rule and
 9 Section 5 of the FTC Act, 15 U.S.C. § 45.
10          34.     The Department of Justice alleged that TikTok’s Musical.ly predecessors had

11 collected and used personal information from children younger than 13 in violation of COPPA,
12 including by (1) failing to directly notify parents of the information it collects online from children
13 under 13 and how it uses such information and (2) failing to obtain verifiable parental consent
14 before any collection or use of personal information from children under 13. United States v.
15 Musical.ly, et al., No. 2:19-cv-01439-ODW-RAO (C.D. Cal. Feb. 27, 2019) (Dkt. No. 1).
16          35.     In March 2019, the Honorable Otis D. Wright II entered a Stipulated Order for Civil

17 Penalties, Permanent Injunction, and Other Relief against TikTok’s predecessors. Id. at Dkt. No. 10
18 (2019 Permanent Injunction).
19          36.     As part of the 2019 Permanent Injunction, TikTok’s predecessors were enjoined

20 from violating the COPPA Rule, including by (1) “failing to make reasonable efforts, taking into
21 account available technology, to ensure that a parent of a child receives direct notice of Defendants’
22 practices with regard to the collection, use, or disclosure of Personal Information from children”
23 and (2) “failing to obtain verifiable parental consent before any collection, use, or disclosure of
24 Personal Information from children.” 2019 Permanent Injunction at 8.
25          37.     In 2019, Muiscal.ly was renamed TikTok Ltd., and Musical.ly Inc. was renamed

26 TikTok Inc. This renaming did not change the companies’ obligations under the 2019 Permanent
27 Injunction.
28

 1          38.     Despite the 2019 injunction, millions of American Children under the age of 13

 2 continue to create accounts on the TikTok platform and continuously have their PII collected and
 3 used without parental notice or verifiable parental consent.
 4          39.     On June 12, 2020 TikTok Inc. stated to the FTC that “[o]n May 11, 2019…[it] took

 5 offline all US accounts that did not go through [its recently imposed] age gate. These
 6 accounts…were not accessible to the Company. TikTok did not use or disclose the information for
 7 any purpose.” TikTok Inc. also stated that it “completed on May 24, 2020” the deletion of
 8 children’s data as required by the 2019 Permanent Injunction. V Pappas, as “GM of TikTok,”
 9 certified on TikTok Inc.’s behalf under penalty of perjury that the prior statement was true and
10 correct.
11          40.     According to the August 2, 2024 DOJ Complaint, after follow-up inquiry by the

12 FTC, TikTok Inc. acknowledged that its June 12, 2020 claims had been false. In fact, TikTok Inc.
13 retained and used data that it previously represented it “did not use,” and was “not accessible” to it,
14 and was “delet[ed].” That data included the personal information and other data of child, teen, and
15 adult users, including IP addresses, device IDs, device models and advertising IDs.
16       B. Defendants’ TikTok Platform and account creation

17          41.     TikTok operates a video-based social media platform that consumers may access via

18 the Internet or through a downloadable software application or “app.”
19          42.     The TikTok platform allows users to create, upload, and share shortform videos. The

20 TikTok app is free to download. It generates revenue for Defendants through advertising and
21 eCommerce, including through the TikTok for Business platform, as well as in-app purchases
22 through TikTok Shop.
23          43.     TikTok features a “For You Page” feed in which an algorithm subject to Defendants’

24 control selects videos for each user based on its determination of their interests, pushes those videos
25 to the user, and plays them.
26          44.     TikTok’s algorithms are trained on data collected from users via the TikTok platform

27 and from third-party sources. Such data include videos viewed, “liked,” or shared, accounts
28

           Case 3:25-cv-01320-JD         Document 1        Filed 02/07/25      Page 9 of 31




 1 followed, comments, content created, video captions, sounds, and hashtags, as well as device and
 2 account settings such as language preference, country setting, and device type.
 3           45.    TikTok was, at all relevant times, aware that minor children accessed and engaged

 4 with its platform and actively sought to increase viewing and engagement by children through
 5 content directed toward those children, while publicly representing that such minors were not
 6 permitted to access TikTok’s adult version and were protected by TikTok Kid’s version.
 7           46.    Since at least March 2019, Defendants have required that users input a birthdate

 8 when creating a TikTok account. This is also known as an age-gate.
 9           47.    Children who self-identify as under the age of 13 in the United States are offered

10 what Defendants refer to as TikTok for Younger Users or “Kids Mode” (hereinafter “Kids Mode”).
11           48.    In Kids Mode, a user can view videos, but cannot upload videos, post information

12 publicly, or message other users.
13           49.    Parents are neither notified nor asked to consent to the creation of an account in Kids

14 Mode.
15           50.    If a user indicates that he or she is over the age of 13, that user is permitted to create

16 a regular account on TikTok.
17           51.    Defendants implemented this “age-gate” in response to the DOJ’s 2019 action

18 discussed above. This age-gate is insufficient. First, kids can make multiple attempts at creating an
19 account, if at first after entering their accurate age enacts the limitations of the functionality of the
20 app, kids can go back in and create a new account changing their age to be over 13, and the app
21 does nothing to stop or prevent this, thus Defendants having actual knowledge of the child user’s
22 age, Defendants permit the children to create a new account circumventing the age-gate.
23           52.    Second, kids were allowed to utilize third party login credentials from Instagram or

24 Google, identifying these child user accounts as “age unknown” accounts. This led to the creation of
25 millions of accounts for which Defendants did not know the age of the user.
26           53.    Regardless of whether a Child uses a regular TikTok account or a Kids Mode

27 account, TikTok violates the COPPA Rule by collecting and using their personal information
28 without parental notice and consent.

 1          54.     TikTok’s insufficient age verification policies resulted in millions of Children

 2 gaining access to regular TikTok accounts and to the adult content and features of a regular TikTok
 3 account.
 4          55.     For Children with regular TikTok accounts, TikTok collects personal information

 5 about them, including first and last name, age, email address, phone number, persistent identifiers
 6 for the device(s) used to access TikTok, social media account information, and profile image(s), as
 7 well as photographs, videos, and audio files containing the user’s image and voice and the metadata
 8 associated with such media (such as when, where, and by whom the content was created), usage
 9 information, device information, location data, image and audio information, metadata, and data
10 from cookies and similar technologies that track users across different websites and platforms.
11          56.     For Children with Kids Mode accounts, TikTok still collects personal information

12 about them, including several types of persistent identifiers, including IP address and unique device
13 identifiers. TikTok also collects app activity data, device information, mobile carrier information,
14 and app information from Children using Kids Mode accounts—which it combines with persistent
15 identifiers and uses to amass profiles on children.
16          57.     Defendants’ practice of allowing children to sign up for a TikTok account using third

17 party credentials allowed children to create a TikTok account, gaining access to adult content and
18 features of the general TikTok platform without providing age information. Without parental notice
19 or consent, Defendants then collected and maintained vast amounts of personal information from
20 the children who created and used these TikTok accounts.
21          58.     In 2022, the loophole utilizing third-party credentials was closed when Defendants

22 required all users to go through the TikTok age-gate. Closing this loop-hole does not fool proof the
23 age-gate strategy.
24      C. The Children’s online Privacy Protection Act of 1998

25          59.     Congress passed COPPA, codified at 15 U.S.C. § 6501, et seq., in 1998 in response

26 to concerns that children’s online activities were being tracked by operators of websites and online
27 services. COPPA is intended to “maintain the security of personally identifiable information of
28 children collected online” and to “protect children’s privacy by limiting the collection of personal
                                               - 10 -
                                      CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
          Case 3:25-cv-01320-JD        Document 1        Filed 02/07/25      Page 11 of 31




 1 information from children without parental consent.”3 The standards in COPPA have given rise to,
 2 and correlate with, accepted norms throughout society for defining the expectations of privacy for
 3 minor children.
 4          60.    COPPA applies to any operator of a commercial website or online service directed to

 5 children under 13 years of age that collects, uses, and/or discloses personal information from
 6 children. The FTC considers parties with actual knowledge that they are collecting personal
 7 information from users of a child-directed site or service as “operators” under COPPA.
 8          61.    COPPA “prohibits unfair … acts or practices in connection with the collection, use,

 9 and/or disclosure of personal information from and about children on the Internet.” 16 C.F.R. §
10 312.1.
11          62.    COPPA provides, in pertinent part, that:

12                 It is unlawful for an operator of a website or online service directed to
                   children, or any operator that has actual knowledge that it is collecting
13                 personal information from a child, to collect personal information from a
                   child in a manner that violates the regulations prescribed [by the Federal
14                 Trade Commission]. 15 U.S.C. § 6502(a).

15          63.    COPPA thus prohibits, inter alia, the collection of persistent identifiers for

16 behavioral advertising absent notice and verifiable parental consent. 16 C.F.R. §§ 312.5(c)(7),
17 312.2.
18          64.    COPPA specifically requires an “operator” covered by COPPA to give notice to

19 parents and obtain their verifiable consent before collecting children’s personal information online.
20 16 C.F.R. §§ 312.4 and 312.5. This includes but is not limited to:
21                 •     Posting a privacy policy on its website or online service providing clear,

22                       understandable, and complete notice of its information practices, including

23                       what information the website operator collects from children online, how it

24                       uses such information, its disclosure practices for such information, and other

25                       specific disclosures set forth by COPPA;

26                 •     Providing clear, understandable, and complete notice of its information

27                       practices, including specific disclosures directly to parents; and

28
                                               - 11 -
                                      CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
            Case 3:25-cv-01320-JD        Document 1        Filed 02/07/25     Page 12 of 31




 1                   •     Obtaining verifiable parental consent prior to collecting, using, and/or

 2                         disclosing personal information from children.

 3            65.    The FTC has interpreted “operators of website or online services directed to

 4 children” and “operators with actual knowledge that they are collecting personal information online
 5 from children under 13” “subject to strict liability for COPPA violations.” 2
 6            66.    Websites or online services that collect personal information from users of other

 7 child directed websites or online services are deemed as “child-directed” if the website or online
 8 service “has actual knowledge that it is collecting personal information directly from users of
 9 another Web site or online service directed to children.” 16 C.F.R. § 312.2.
10            67.    In order to determine whether a website or online service is “directed to children” the

11 FTC will:
12                   [C]onsider [the website’s or online service’s] subject matter, visual
                     content, use of animated characters or child-oriented activities and
13                   incentives, music or other audio content, age of models, presence of child
                     celebrities or celebrities who appeal to children, language or other
14                   characteristics of the Web site or online service, as well as whether
15                   advertising promoting or appearing on the Web site or online service is
                     directed to children.
16         16 FR § 312.2

17            68.    In 2013, COPPA was enhanced (the “2013 COPPA Enhancement”) to provide

18 further protection for children against online tracking and to “giv[e] parents greater control over the
19 online collection of their children’s personal information.” The 2013 enhancement widened the
20 definition of children’s “personal information” to include “persistent identifiers” such as cookies
21 that track a child’s activity online, geolocation information, photos, videos, and audio recordings.
22            69.    The 2013 COPPA Enhancement was the culmination of two years of rulemaking by

23 the FTC and reflected society’s growing recognition of the surreptitious surveillance tactics used by
24 advertising companies to track children online and advertise to them while using the internet.
25
26

         Statement of Joseph J. Simons & Christine S. Wilson, Regarding FTC and People of the State of

 1           70.    By expressly including persistent identifiers and geolocation data in COPPA’s

 2 definition of personal information, the FTC intended to deter advertising companies and internet
 3 operators such as Defendants from exploiting young children via tracking, profiling, and advertising
 4 online.
 5           71.    Pursuant to Section 1303(c) of COPPA, 15 U.S.C. § 6502(c), and Section 18(d)(3) of

 6 the FTC Act, 15 U.S.C. § 57a(d)(3), a violation of COPPA constitutes an unfair … act or practice in
 7 or affecting commerce in violation of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act, 15 U.S.C. § 45(a).
 8           72.    While COPPA does not itself provide a private right of action for individuals to seek

 9 redress for harms arising from COPPA violations, and contains a limited preemption clause barring
10 the imposition of liability by states and local governments “inconsistent” with COPPA (15 U.S.C. §
11 6502(d)), the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit has held that “COPPA’s
12 preemption clause does not bar state-law causes of action that are parallel to, or proscribe the same
13 conduct forbidden by, COPPA.” Jones v. Google LLC, 73 F.4th 636 (9th Cir. 2023).
14           73.    Therefore, individuals harmed by conduct which violates COPPA such as the

15 conduct described herein may seek redress for harms via state law causes of action.
16      D. Plaintiff’s experience

17           74.    At all relevant times, Plaintiff had a TikTok account and was under the age of 13.
